title: CrabRAG: Why Automated Assistants Need Graph Memory, Not More Tokens — Stephen Chin, Neo4j
talk_summary: Speaker argues markdown/vector-only agent memory wastes tokens and fails multi-hop queries; he demos a Neo4j/Cognee graph memory that uses vector seeds plus graph traversal to retrieve precise, auditable context. The evidence is a home-lab digital-twin demo, not a controlled benchmark.

takeaways.what_they_do: Store entities, relationships, and actions as graph nodes/edges; use vector search only to find seed nodes, then traverse and rank neighbors before injecting the selected subgraph into context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: uses the vector search to get the seed nodes where it starts the traversal. And then it uses a graph search

takeaways.technique: Write actions to graph, traverse instead of re-read
takeaways.what_they_do: Have the agent log each action/result into the graph as it works; later sessions query/traverse that graph rather than re-reading full transcripts or files.
takeaways.evidence_quote: have Claude write each action into the graph as he works. We're going to follow up by traversing, not re-reading it.

takeaways.what_they_do: The speaker claims markdown-file memory causes agents to repeatedly load large, mostly irrelevant context every round.
takeaways.evidence_quote: average agents are loading up at least 100k in tokens for each round.

takeaways.technique: Code dependency graph for PR review
takeaways.what_they_do: Use graph relationships to answer multi-hop questions that similarity search misses, such as impacted callers, tests, and dependencies.
takeaways.evidence_quote: those large multi-hop reasoning chains don't work on similarity searches.

takeaways.technique: Memory as a scoped MCP/plugin service
takeaways.what_they_do: Expose memory operations as a pluggable MCP server with retrieve/remember/forget commands, while warning that forget can wipe memory.
takeaways.evidence_quote: treats memory just like another MCP server
